idea: When to replace old plumbing pipes
title: Identifying Internal Corrosion in Galvanized Steel Piping
description: An educational guide explaining how internal tuberculation in older galvanized steel pipes restricts water flow despite a intact outer appearance, serving as a primary indicator for pipe replacement.
image_prompt: A professional macro photograph showing a clean cross-sectional cut of an old 3/4-inch galvanized steel plumbing pipe, set in a clean plumbing workbench environment. Vertical 9:16 aspect ratio. The main subject is centered: the cut pipe wall reveals heavy internal tuberculation, with dark reddish-brown iron oxide rust and mineral scale restricting the inner bore by more than half, while the outer galvanized exterior shows only minor surface dullness. Positioned neatly beside it is a short cut section of clean, modern copper or PEX pipe to provide clear visual material contrast. Realistic metallic textures, sharp focus on internal pipe scale, soft professional side lighting with high detail, neutral gray background. No text, no visual labels, no graphics, no logos, no watermarks, no fake brand names, no artificial arrows.
visual_story: The visual focuses on the stark difference between a pipe's exterior shell and its internal waterway. Viewers immediately notice the severe rust buildup inside the cut galvanized pipe cross-section, showing how mineral scale blocks water passage. Placing a clean pipe cut section next to it highlights lost internal diameter. This visual directly supports the lesson by demonstrating why visual outer inspection alone is insufficient to evaluate old metal piping.

on_image_text.hook: Low Water Flow Isn't Always a Valve Problem
on_image_text.explanation: Galvanized steel pipes corrode from the inside out, accumulating dense iron oxide rust that shrinks the internal pipe diameter over time.
on_image_text.takeaway: When fixture flow drops system-wide despite normal static pressure, inspect internal pipe condition for replacement.
